{{short description|On the rate of convergence of the continued fraction expansion of a typical real number}}
In [[number theory]], '''Lochs's theorem''' concerns the [[rate of convergence]] of the [[continued fraction]] expansion of a typical [[real number]]. A proof of the theorem was published in 1964 by [[Gustav Lochs]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Lochs
 | first = Gustav
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02993063
 | journal = Abhandlungen aus dem Mathematischen Seminar der Universität Hamburg
 | language = German
 | mr = 0162753
 | pages = 142–144
 | title = Vergleich der Genauigkeit von Dezimalbruch und Kettenbruch
 | volume = 27
 | year = 1964
| issue = 1–2
 | s2cid = 119419559
 }}</ref>

The theorem states that for [[almost all]] real numbers in the interval (0,1), the number of terms ''m'' of the number's continued fraction expansion that are required to determine the first ''n'' places of the number's decimal expansion behaves [[asymptotically]] as follows:

:<math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{m}{n}=\frac{6\ln(2)\ln(10)}{\pi^2} \approx 0.97027014</math> {{OEIS|id=A086819}}.<ref>{{MathWorld|urlname=LochsTheorem|title=Lochs' Theorem}}</ref>

As this limit is only slightly smaller than 1, this can be interpreted as saying that each additional term in the continued fraction representation of a "typical" real number increases the accuracy of the representation by approximately one decimal place. The [[decimal]] system is the last [[positional system]] for which each digit carries less information than one continued fraction quotient; going to [[Undecimal|base-11]] (changing <math>\ln(10)</math> to <math>\ln(11)</math> in the equation) makes the above value exceed 1.

The reciprocal of this limit,

:<math>\frac{\pi^2}{6\ln(2)\ln(10)} \approx 1.03064083</math> {{OEIS|id=A062542}},

is twice the base-10 [[logarithm]] of [[Lévy's constant]].

[[File:Lochs' theorem golden ratio.svg|thumb|400px|alt=Plot of number of continued fraction coefficients versus number of decimal digits, for three "typical" random numbers exhibiting the typical behavior, contrasted with the golden ratio, which requires noticeably more coefficients per digit.|Three typical numbers, and the [[golden ratio]]. The typical numbers follow an approximately 45° line, since each continued fraction coefficient yields approximately one decimal digit. The golden ratio, on the other hand, is the number requiring the most coefficients for each digit.]]

A prominent example of a number not exhibiting this behavior is the [[golden ratio]]—sometimes known as the "[[Continued fraction#A property of the golden ratio φ|most irrational]]" number—whose continued fraction terms are all ones, the smallest possible in canonical form. On average it requires

:<math>\frac{1}{\log_{10}(1+\varphi)} \approx 2.39248598  </math> {{OEIS|id=A392067}} per decimal digit. <ref>{{cite news|last1=Cooper|first1=Harold|title=Continued Fraction Streams|newspaper=Exist |date=17 August 2016 |url=https://x.st/continued-fraction-streams/#lochs-theorem|accessdate=30 August 2016}}</ref>

{{clear}}

== Proof ==

The proof assumes basic properties of [[Continued fraction#Some useful theorems|continued fractions]].
Let <math>T : x \mapsto 1/x \mod 1</math> be the [[Gauss map]].

Let <math>\rho(t) = \frac{1}{(1+t)\ln 2}</math> be the [[probability density function]] for the Gauss distribution, which is preserved under the Gauss map.

Since the probability density function is bounded above and below, a set is negligible with respect to the [[Lebesgue measure]] [[if and only if]] to the Gauss distribution.

=== Lemma ===
'''Lemma.''' <math display="inline">\frac 1n \ln T^n x \to 0</math>.

'''Proof.''' Since <math display="inline">T^nx \leq 1</math>, we have <math display="inline">\frac 1n \ln T^n x \to 0</math> if and only if<math display="block">
          \liminf\frac 1n \ln T^n x = 0
          </math>Let us consider the set of all <math display="inline">x</math> that have <math display="inline">\liminf\frac 1n \ln T^n x < 0</math>. That is,<math display="block">
          \{x : \exists c > 0, \forall N \geq 1, \exists n \geq N, T^n x < e^{-cn}\}
          </math> <math display="block">
          = \cup_{c > 0} \cap_{N \geq 1} \cup_{n \geq N} [0; \N, \dots, \N, a_n > e^{cn}, \N, \dots]
          </math>where <math>[0; \N, \dots, \N, a_n > e^{cn}, \N, \dots]</math> denotes the set of numbers whose continued fraction expansion has <math>a_n > e^{cn} </math>, but no other constraints. 
Now, since the Gauss map preserves the Gauss measure,<math display="block">[0; \N, \dots, \N, a_n > e^{cn}, \N, \dots]</math>has the same Gauss measure as <math display="inline">[0; a_n > e^{cn}, \N, \dots]</math>, which is the same as

<math display="block">
          \int_0^{e^{-cn}} \rho(t)dt = \log_2(1+e^{-cn})\sim \frac{e^{-cn}}{\ln 2}
          </math>The union over <math display="inline">\cup_{n \geq N}</math> sums to <math display="inline">\sim \frac{e^{-cN}}{(1-e^{-c})\ln 2}</math>, which at the <math display="inline">N\to\infty</math> limit is zero.

Thus the set of such <math display="inline">x</math> has Gauss measure zero.

=== Finish the estimate ===
Now, expand the term using basic continued fraction properties:<math display="block">\ln\left|
 x - \frac{p_n}{q_n}
 \right| = \ln \frac{T^n x}{q_n(q_n + q_{n-1}T^n x )} = - 2\ln q_n + \ln T^n x -  \ln\left(1 + \frac{q_{n-1}}{q_n}T^n x \right)</math>The second is <math display="inline">o(n)</math>. The third term is <math display="inline">\in [\ln 1, \ln 2]</math>. Both disappear after dividing by <math>n</math>.<br />Thus<math display="block">\lim_{n} \frac 1n \ln\left|
 x - \frac{p_n}{q_n}
 \right| = -2 \lim_n \frac 1n  \ln q_n = -\frac{\pi^2}{6\ln 2}  </math>where we used the result from [[Lévy's constant]].
